questions.title_en: Amen to a Chazzan with a different pronunciation of Hebrew
questions.question:
It is forbidden for a chazzan to lead a congregation that distinguishes between more letters than he does.

Thus, if one is praying at a minyan where the chazzan's pronunciation is less exacting than the congregation's, should one answer Amen?

Why/why not? If so, is it for the same reason that he shouldn't be chazzan in the first place?

As of now, this is theoretical, but my current situation makes it very possible that I might end up with such a problem.

answers.text:
That's not the correct interpretation of the source you brought. There's no such abstract concept that the chazzan can't lead a congregation that distinguishes more letters than he does.

Rather, it is inappropriate to appoint in permanent fashion a chazzan who cannot properly pronounce the words. (SA,OC 53:12). See Mishna Berurah there who points out a view (Pri Chadash) that if there is no more fitting chazzan, even if he pronounces the hei and ches equivalently, he may be appointed. Note also that in the Beiur Halacha there, he says that we should also be stringent with this on a non-permanent basis.

Note also that the Taz in SA, OC 128:33 says that this is not considered a disqualifying factor for a chazzan or kohen (this rule also applies to a kohen duchaning) because רוב עמינו אין יודעים להבחין בזה

questions.title_en: Saying Shehechiyanu on new glasses
questions.question:
When one purchases a new pair of glasses, does one need to say Shehechiyanu on them like one would on a new suit?

Following that, is it permissible to buy them in the Omer or The Three Weeks, assuming they aren't medically necessary?

answers.text:
Saying שהחיינו

On the Dirshu site there's an answer by רבי מרדכי הלוי שוורצבורד who decides that since spectacles are worn to correct a medical "issue", one does not say שהחיינו.

המשקפיים הינם כלי עזר רפואי להתמודד עם בעיית ליקוי ראיה, לכן אין לברך עליהם שהחיינו.‏

On the Kipa site there's an answer by הרב שלמה בן אליהו who explains that one theoretically should say שהחיינו but since they are for a medical "issue" the custom is not to say it.

מעיקר הדין היה צריך לברך אם שמחים כמובן.‏ אבל לא נהגו לברך שהחינו על כל פגיעה בבריאות, כי התרופה והמשקפים באו לעולם בעצם בגלל החולשה ופגם הראות אז איננו מברכים על כך שהחינו.‏

(Unsure if these first 2 answers are identical)

The Etz Chaim site brings an answer by הרב יקותיאל אוהב ציון with various opinions, but he decides that one should say שהחיינו, since one feels joy when buying a new pair.

תשובה בקיצור: כל דבר שהאדם שמח בקנייתו מברך עליו שהחיינו, ואפילו אם רוב האנשים לא שמחים באותו דבר, כיון שהאדם שמח, לא ימנע מלברך שהחיינו על שמחתו, ויש בזה שבח ויקר לכבוד ה’ יתברך, ועל כן גם אדם הזקוק למשקפיים או שינים תותבות וכיו”ב, כיון שעכשיו יש לו הנאה ושמחה, מברך שהחיינו. ‏

נימוקים ומקורות:‏

א. הנה דין ברכת שהחיינו הוא בכל כלי חדש או בגד שהאדם שמח בו, וכבר כתבנו במקום אחר, שבזמנינו שיש חשיבות לנעליים, אזי יש לברך שהחיינו גם על נעליים חדשות אם שמח בהם, וכדמוכח בדברי התוס’ בברכות (נט ע”ב) ובלשון השו”ע (סי’ רכג ס”ו). וכך הורה מרן הגר”ד קוק שליט”א. וכעת אין להרחיב בזה.‏

ביאור צדדי הספק

ב. ובענין משקפיים יש לשאול, שהרי הצורך במשקפיים הוא מחמת לקות הראיה, וכל אדם מצד רצונו האישי היה מעדיף שלא להזדקק למשקפיים, רק שבעל כרחו מפני בעיית הראיה הוא קונה אותם, ואם כן אולי יש לומר שעל דבר כזה לא מברכים שהחיינו. וזה ברור לכאורה שחרש הקונה מכשיר שמיעה לא מברך שהחיינו, וגם אם יצפה את המכשיר בזהב טהור, הרי בודאי היה מעדיף להיות בריא ולשמוע ככל האדם, ובעל כרחו שלא בטובתו הוא קונה מכשיר כדי שיוכל לשמוע יותר טוב. ואם כן הוא הדין לכאורה במשקפיים.‏

דברי גאון עזינו הגר”ד קוק שליט”א

ג. וגאון עזינו הגר”ד קוק שליט”א אמר לי, שענין זה תלוי לכאורה במחלוקת רש”י ותוס’ בגדר “מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה”, דרש”י בשבת (צג ע”ב) ביאר שברצונו היה מעדיף שלא תעשה המלאכה, אבל התוס’ לא ניחא להו בפירוש זה, דסוף סוף השתא ניחא ליה בעל כרחו, שהרי יודע עכשיו שלא יגיע לרצונו בלא המלאכה, ולכן פירשו התוס’ שאדם העושה מלאכה ואין תכליתו כמו תכליתה במשכן, זהו גדר מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה. הרי לפנינו שנחלקו רש”י ותוס’ אם מתחשבים ברצון המקיף של האדם מה היה רוצה אילו היה הדבר בידו, או דאזלינן בתר השתא ובאשר הוא שם, ואם עכשיו זהו רצונו, אזי המצב העכשווי הוא הקובע. ולפי”ז יש לומר דלדברי התוס’ יש לברך שהחיינו, ולדברי רש”י יש מקום לומר דלא יברך. [כיון שיש לצדד דגדרי מלאכות שבת לחוד, והלכות ברכות השבח לחוד. ודו”ק].‏

Permissiblity to buy them in the Omer or three weeks

During the Omer the classic Halachic books (Shulchan Aruch, Kitzur and others) do not mention that there's a custom not to buy new clothing or not to say שהחיינו - so there should not be an issue.

During the 3 weeks the custom is not to say שהחיינו and thus, if one decides that buying new glasses warrants a שהחיינו, then one should probably refrain from buying them. If one cannot function without them then CLOR, as one would expect it to be allowed - since we do say שהחיינו under extenuating circumstances.

questions.title_en: Why Pharaoh of Exodus, in Ezekiel 29:3?
questions.question:
Ezekiel 29:3:

"Speak these words: Thus said the Sovereign GOD:
I am going to deal with you, O Pharaoh king of Egypt,
Mighty monster, sprawling in your channels,
Who said,
My Nile is my own;
I made it for myself."

According to Bereshit Rabbah 100:1, The pharaoh referred to, is the pharaoh of the Exodus!

“Know that the Lord is God” (Psalms 100:3) – Rabbi Yehuda bar Simon and Rabbi Aḥa, Rabbi Yehuda bar Simon said: “Know that the Lord is God, He made us, and we did not [velo]” (Psalms 100:3) create ourselves, unlike Pharaoh, who said: “My river is mine and I made myself” (Ezekiel 29:3). Rabbi Aḥa said: “Know that the Lord is God, He made us and to Him [velo]” we devote ourselves.

This is repeated in other midrash as well. e.g.,

Midrash Tanchuma Buber, Vaera 8:1:

Another interpretation (of Exod. 7:1) SEE, I HAVE SET YOU AS A GOD TO PHARAOH. The Holy One said: Because he made himself into a god, they informed him that he was nothing in the world. See, I have made you a god over him. And where is it shown that Pharaoh made himself into a god? Where it is stated (of Pharaoh in Ezek. 29:3): {BECAUSE HE} [WHO] SAID {THE} [MY] NILE IS MY OWN, AND I MADE MYSELF. I am the one who created myself.

As well as: Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Amalek 3:40; Mekhilta DeRabbi Shimon Ben Yochai...etc.

Why did the Rabbis refer to the pharaoh of Ezekiel as the pharaoh of Exodus?

answers.text:
Meir has brought an answer that has all the information you need to answer the question.

Firstly, the Bereshit Rabbah doesn't seem to mention anything about the Exodus? Just want to get that out of the way.

However the other midrash does, but that's because when the Torah doesn't give a name, it is telling us a unified idea (based on Zohar II, 34a). In this case, it is the idea that the Pharaohs of Egypt represent the concept of supreme arrogance, to the point of feeling they are disconnected from Hashem, and indeed made themselves, and Ezekiel is Hashem's response to this.

It doesn't matter which Pharoah you pick, but we do have a lot of material on the Pharaoh of Egypt, so the midrash draws information to substantiate and expand on its lesson.

This is what midrash does. It isn't necessarily saying "the Pharaoh in Ezekiel 29 is the one from the Exodus" as some sort of historical fact, but as a "drash", i.e. an interprative lesson.

Interestingly, the Pharaohs didn't refer to themselves as such, but rather as "kings", which supports this interpration. The Torah is viewed as the main reason we call them such in today's day. Much of what we know from historical data about the Pharaohs of this time corroborates this Zohar that the Pharaohs viewed themselves as gods.

questions.title_en: Wedge in between toes on shabbos
questions.question:
One of the common ways to treat an ingrown toenail is to place a small rubber or plastic wedge in between the toe that is infected and the next toe to give it space and not apply pressure on the infected area.

This doesn't necessarily heal it, rather could just be there to provide relief for the individual, since the infected toe is not being pushed against its neighbouring toe.

Would this be an issue to wear on Shabbat (in a reshus harabim or to walk from one reshus to another) due to the fact that it's not a piece of clothing and there's a possibility it will fall out from between ones toes and become loose in the sock or shoe?

answers.text: Seems like it might be similar to a wad of soft material placed inside a shoe (for a foot injury or just to pad it for comfort), where if the shoe is completely enclosed, it's fine without tying the wad in place (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 303:15). The Baal Hatanya, in his formulation of this halachah (303:17), adds that "it's like an ornament or clothing, since it serves the body's comfort just like any garment."

Shmirat Shabbat K'Hilchata (18:21) allows one to carry in the public domain

  • orthopedic supports inside one's shoes (but not in open sandals unless the support is firmly attached)
  • insoles to keep feet warm, absorb perspiration or provide a better fit

Commentators (e.g., Mishna Brura Ohr Olam to 303:48) explain this is permitted because (1) the inserts are not seen by others so there is no issue of marit ayin and (2) it is evident one is not doing it as a ploy, to transport the insert. R Shlomo Zalman Auerbach adds that they are manufactured for that objective only. See also Igrot Moshe OC 1:107.

All these reasons appear to permit the wedge you are asking about. From personal experience, I can say they rarely fall when properly set, of the proper size and worn with socks. Should they fall it would be a case of ones.

Of course, consult your rabbi before implementing anything you learn here.

questions.title_en: How can "Lo Sasur" be used as a primary source for the power of rabbinic legislation?
questions.question:
The context of "Lo Sasur" is that when the law isn't clear the kohanim (and the shofet) at the mikdash are the final authority. See Devarim 17:8-11

(ח) כִּי יִפָּלֵא מִמְּךָ דָבָר לַמִּשְׁפָּט בֵּין דָּם לְדָם בֵּין דִּין לְדִין וּבֵין נֶגַע לָנֶגַע דִּבְרֵי רִיבֹת בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ וְקַמְתָּ וְעָלִיתָ אֶל הַמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יִבְחַר י"י אֱלֹהֶיךָ בּוֹ. (ט) וּבָאתָ אֶל הַכֹּהֲנִים הַלְוִיִּם וְאֶל הַשֹּׁפֵט אֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם וְדָרַשְׁתָּ וְהִגִּידוּ לְךָ אֵת דְּבַר הַמִּשְׁפָּט. (י) וְעָשִׂיתָ עַל פִּי הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר יַגִּידוּ לְךָ מִן הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא אֲשֶׁר יִבְחַר י"י וְשָׁמַרְתָּ לַעֲשׂוֹת כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר יוֹרוּךָ. (יא) עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה אֲשֶׁר יוֹרוּךָ וְעַל הַמִּשְׁפָּט אֲשֶׁר יֹאמְרוּ לְךָ תַּעֲשֶׂה לֹא תָסוּר מִן הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר יַגִּידוּ לְךָ יָמִין וּשְׂמֹאל.

(8) If there arises a matter too hard for you in judgment, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, being matters of controversy within your gates; then you shall arise, and go up to the place which Hashem your God shall choose. (9) And you shall come to the priests, the Levites, and to the judge who shall be in those days: and you shall inquire; and they shall tell you the matter of judgment. (10) You shall do according to the matter which they shall tell you from that place which Hashem shall choose; and you shall observe to do according to all that they shall teach you. (11) According to the teaching which they shall teach you, and according to the judgment which they shall tell you, you shall do; you shall not turn aside from the matter which they shall show you, to the right hand, nor to the left.

Chazal famously use this as the primary source for the rabbinic power to enact new legislation (ie takanos, gezeiros, etc)

As peshuto shel mikra refers to the adjudication of difficult cases, (see eg R A ibn Ezra על פי התורה אשר יורוך – בדבר המופלא. ACCORDING TO THE LAW WHICH THEY SHALL TEACH THEE. With regard to the matter that is too hard for you) how can Chazal use this as the source for their legislative ability when the plain meaning and context refers to judicial authority only?

(Qualification: this seems to be an issue for Rambam only, who understands [ShM Shoresh 1]—as b Shab 23 seems to indicate—that Lo Sasur also includes freestanding rabbinic legislation. Ramban vehemently disagrees. He is of the opinion that only rabbinic explanations of the Torah [via interpreting a word's meaning and wielding the middos shehatorah nidreshes bahem] are covered by Lo Sasur, takanos and gezeiros are most assuredly not.)

answers.text:
I think you're having difficulty because your premise is incorrect.

The basis for enacting new legislation actually comes from an injunction to do so found in Vayikra 18:30:

ושמרתם את משמרתי לבלתי עשות מחקות התועבות אשר נעשו לפניכם ולא תטמאו בהם אני ה' א-להיכם

And you shall observe My charge, not to commit any of the abominable practices that were done before you, and you shall not become defiled by them. I am the Lord your God.

Rashi there says:

להזהיר בית דין על כך

To exhort the courts about this.

The Gra says:

לעשות משמרת למשמרת

To make a guarding for the guarding.

In other words, to enact further decrees to set up "guardrails" against the commandments.

Seforno, in greater detail, says:

שמרו גם את המצות שצויתי לשמירה וגדר שלא תכשלו בכל אלה, כמו אסורי מאכלות וטומאת נדה וזבה ויולדת וזולתם, ובזה האופן לא תטמאו בהם:

Also guard the commandments which I commanded as a protection and "guardrail," so that you won't stumble in these. For example, forbidden foods, ritual impurities of niddah/zavah/postpartum and others. In this way you won't become impure through them.

In other words, the Torah itself instructs Chazal to make guardrails. The setting up of additional injunctions by Chazal is a direct and explicit commandment, outside of the judicial authority granted to them by the Torah.

1. rabbinic legitimacy
  2. rabbinic laws

the first cannot necessarily be derived from what you may interpret as you wish. the rabbis can be trusted to derive the second if the first is true.

(by the way, if you take a verses plain meaning to mean 1), and the rabbis say that we know 2) from the verse, than if you still have 1) after, you have also 2). also, i don't think polemics against adversaries can be used as legitimate within the system.)

questions.title_he: לעבוד כמנהלת חשבונות במקום שמוכרים לא כשר
questions.question:
אני מנהלת חשבונות ורציתי לדעת אם מותר לעבוד במקום שמוכר לא כשר 
אני לא באה במגע עם הסחורה

שלום
סליחה על העיכוב במתן התשובה.
מעיקר הדין מותר לעבוד במקום כזה, ומכל מקום אם אפשר עדיף למצוא עבודה אחרת כשרה לחלוטין.
הרחבות ומקורות
הרי גם אם את לא תלכי לעבוד שם ימצאו מישהי אחרת שתעשה את העבודה, ובאופן כזה לא שייך האיסור שכתוב בתורה (ויקרא יט יד) "לפני עיוור לא תיתן מכשול", וכמבואר במסכת עבודה זרה (דף ו עמוד ב).
אמנם יש דעות שבכל זאת יש בזה איסור מדרבנן משום מסייע בידי עוברי עבירה, והרמ"א יורה דעה (סימן קנא סעיף א) כתב, שכל בעל נפש יחמיר לעצמו.
אך יש לסייג את הדברים. למי שאינו בא במגע עם האוכל אין שום איסור לנהל חנות שמוכרת אוכל שאינו כשר. אמנם כל זה נכון במקרה שבעל המסעדה/המקום היה גוי, אבל במקרה שבעל המסעדה הוא יהודי, יש כאן בעיה של מסייע בידי עוברי עבירה שהרי אסור לסחור במאכלות אסורות, אמנם יש להתיר משום שי"א שאין איסור מסייע בישראל שבכל מקרה יעבור את העבירה (ש"ך יורה דעה, סי' קנ"א ס"ק ו', ודגול מרבבה שם), ובמקרה (כמו שלך, נראה) שגם אם תאמרי לבעלים שאסור לסחור במאכלות אסורות הוא לא יפסיק למכור, ואת לא יכולה להשפיע עליו ולהפרישו מאיסור, אלא הוא ימצא אדם אחר שינהל לו את העסק ובאדם שהוא מומר לענין זה ועושה את העבירה במזיד יש מקילים שאין בזה איסור מסייע. (וכפי שכתב בזה בשו"ת ציץ אליעזר חי"ט סי' ל"ג, על פי שו"ת מחנה חיים חלק א' סי' מ"ה).
כמו כן, כאן הסיוע ניתן שלא בשעת העבירה, ועל כך יש דעות בגדולי הפוסקים (שו"ת בנין ציון סימן טו, ושו"ת כתב סופר חלק יורה דעה סימן פג) שאין בזה אפילו איסור מסייע מדרבנן. ויעויין בשו"ת יביע אומר חלק ב' (חלק אורח חיים סימן טו אות יד) ובשו"ת ציץ אליעזר חלק כ"א (סימן יד אות ד) שצירפו דעות אלו להקל בנידון שלהם שם. 
כאמור, כל זה מעיקר הדין, וניתן לסמוך על כך. אולם אם היא יכולה למצוא עבודה אחרת כשרה לחלוטין בוודאי שכך עדיף יותר.
יום טוב

questions.title_en: Havdallah after Pesach
questions.question:
The Koren Machsor states that some have the custom to say Havdalah on beer after Pesach.

  1. Any idea how this could be done as a practical matter? Buy the beer before Pesach, sell it with your chametz, and then wait the extra hour or 2 for the chametz to be "repurchased" before you make Havdalah? Buy the beer after Pesach before Havdalah? Neither seems to be the practical basis for a minhag.

  2. Anybody know of a source for the minhag?

thank you.

answers.text: The Rama mentions this custom (OC 296:2). Widespread instantaneous home chametz sales didn't exist back then so presumably the custom was to buy some beer from the local gentiles on the way home from synagogue. That's indeed how people I know who do this go about it.

Havdalah on Motzei Pesach at https://shulchanaruchharav.com/halacha/havdalah-on-motzei-pesach/ states as follows:

Havdalah on Motzei Pesach:

The order of Havdalah follows the same order as any Motzei Yom Tov, or Motzei Shabbos if Yom Tov fell on Shabbos]. See Chapter 13 Halacha 11!

Beer:[1] It is accustomed to be lenient to make Havdalah over beer on Motzei Pesach even if one has much wine at home available.[2] Nevertheless, if the beer is not currently beloved to the person, it is better to make Havdalah over wine even on Motzei Pesach. Furthermore, the above allowance only applies in those areas that beer is considered a significant drink. [The Chabad custom is not to make Havdalah on beer on Motzei Pesach.[3]]

{N.B.: The note in square brackets is in the original}

[1] Admur 296:10; Rama 296:2

[2] As at that time the beer is more beloved to a person than is wine. [ibid]

Other Opinions: Some Poskim rule based on Kabala that one is to always say Havdalah over wine rather than other beverages even if the beer is more beloved. [Kaf Hachaim 296:26]

[3] Otzer Minhagei Chabad Pesach p. 238

questions.title_en: Order of holding Tzitzis by Krias Shma
questions.question:
The Lubavitcher Rebbe writes in Hayom Yom of 22 Sivan:

לאמירת והביאנו לשלום כו' מחברים תחלה ב' הציציות דלפניו, אח"כ [אחר כך] מצרפים ציצית כנף השמאלי דלאחוריו, אח"ז [אחר זה] ציצית דכנף הימין ואוחזים אותם בין קמיצה לזרת דיד שמאל.

In Ahavat olam (p. 44-5), at the words vehavi'einu leshalom, bring together the two front tzitzit. Then join to them the tzitzit of the left back corner, then the tzitzit of the right back corner, holding them together between the little finger and ring finger of the left hand.

  1. What is the rationale behind this order of taking hold of Tzitzis?

  2. Is there another Minhag that says otherwise?

  3. If one is left handed does one reverse this order or does this have nothing to do with Itur Yad?

  4. Which hand does one hold the Tzitzis in if one is left handed?

questions.title_en: Pharaoh made himself according to "Ezekiel 29:3"?
questions.question:
Ezekiel 29:3 Speak these words: Thus said the Sovereign GOD: I am going to deal with you, O Pharaoh king of Egypt, Mighty monster, sprawling in your channels, Who said, My Nile is my own; I made it [for] myself.

*Bereshit Rabbah 100:1 “Know that the Lord is God” (Psalms 100:3) – Rabbi Yehuda bar Simon and Rabbi Aḥa, Rabbi Yehuda bar Simon said: “Know that the Lord is God, He made us, and we did not [velo]” (Psalms 100:3) create ourselves, unlike Pharaoh, who said: “My river is mine and I made myself” (Ezekiel 29:3). Rabbi Aḥa said: “Know that the Lord is God, He made us and to Him [velo]” we devote ourselves.

Midrash Tanchuma Buber, Vaera 8:1 Another interpretation (of Exod. 7:1) SEE, I HAVE SET YOU AS A GOD TO PHARAOH. The Holy One said: Because he made himself into a god, they informed him that he was nothing in the world. See, I have made you a god over him. And where is it shown that Pharaoh made himself into a god? Where it is stated (of Pharaoh in Ezek. 29:3): {BECAUSE HE} [WHO] SAID {THE} [MY] NILE IS MY OWN, AND I MADE MYSELF. I am the one who created myself.*

Why did the midrash interpret the words of the pharaoh in the verse as "I made myself - created myself" instead of " I made it (the river) myself." ?

answers.text:
The wording is וַאֲנִי עֲשִׂיתִנִי which means "I formed myself" (it is a poetic contraction of עשיתי אותי, I made myself).

Translations (Koren, JPS, Kaplan), in order to fit with the rest of the verse, infer a hidden "it". I made [it] myself. Some imagine that ואני is really ולי - for me, as in "I made [it] for me". This is not a simple reading though. Artscroll translates it as "I made myself [powerful]" after Rashi.

The commentators split up the pasuk into two parts. Firstly, "My River is my own", and secondly, separately, "I made myself" (which could also mean, via simple meaning, that I am a self-made man, rather than I created myself, without God's help).

The only way that would have been the simple meaning would have been if it had said ולי, or עשיתיו (or עשיתיהו) instead of עשיתני.

questions.question:
לרב שלום!
פעלתי כהצעת הרב, אך שתי הקבוצות התעקשו. שמצד אחד רוצים שאבחר צד ושמצד שני כדבריהם - לא לנסות להשלים ביניהם, כי הם כבר בוגרים להחליט מה הם רוצים ועם מי הם רוצים או לא רוצים להיות. חשבתי לעבור דירה, אך מבחינת מגבלותיי זה המיקום הטוב ביותר עבורי כרגע. מה עליי לעשות?

שלום
כפי שכתבתי בתשובה הקודמת, נראה לי הכי נכון שאתה מצדך מתנהג בחברות כלפי כל החברים, ולא נכנס למחלוקת ולמריבה שלהם.
פעם תהיה עם קבוצה זו ופעם הקבוצה השניה. אם זה יפריע למישהו מהם, תבקש שלא יערבו אותך ויתנו לך להתנהל לפי רצונותיך, וכפי שאתה לא כופה את דעתך עליהם, שהם לא יכפו את דעתם עליך.
בהצלחה רבה.

questions.title_he: שגיאות כתיב מביכות אצל גדולי עולם
questions.question:
שלום הרב. 
רציתי לשאול איך זה הגיוני שיש אצל השפה של הראשונים והאחרונים צורת ביטוי כל כך תמוהה בלא מובנת? אני שאלתי חברים שנמצאים בישיבה כמה שנים ורבנים והם אמרו לי שצריך פשוט לזרום עם השפה ולהבין את העיקרון. אך זה לא גורם לי לשלווה אלא להפך. איך אנשים גדולי עולם כאלה שעברו על הש"ס מאות פעמים וחברו חיבורים גאונים עליו יכולים לטעות במילות קישור? בכתיבה כה מסורבלת שמצריכה ממני זמן ומאמץ ללמוד את הלשון של כל פרשן ופרשן? 
אני מרגיש שבמקום ללמוד תורה אני מבזבז את זמני (כפשוטו) על הבל. עובדה שכשה"שוטנשטיין" מסביר את הראשונים והאחרונים בהערותיו זה הרבה יוצר ברור. 
ואני לא חושב שזה בגלל שהכתבים עתיקים. גם בתקופתם הם לא היו ברורים. 

מאחר שלא נתת דוגמה לדבריך, אינני יודע למה בדיוק התכוונת, ואולם כלל זה יהיה נקוט בידיך: לא ברור שמה שאתה רואה כשגיאה הוא אכן שגיאה.
זאת משום שכללי הדקדוק וכו' של ימינו, אינם משקפים את כללי דקדוק המקרא המקוריים; ממש לא - רחוק מזה.
לעניין זה דוגמאות רבות מאוד - אסתפק בשתיים: 
א. התנ"ך רחוק מלהקפיד על זכר ונקבה, וכפי שהראה לא פעם פרשן המקרא "רודף הפשט", ראב"ע.  היום זה לא היה "עובר"...
ב. התנ"ך מתבטא לעתים, ביחס למילה זהה הן כזכר והן כנקבה.  גם זה היום לא היה "עובר"... 
הוא שאמרנו: את הדקדוק ואת התחביר המקראי, אין להשתית על דקדוק ימינו, ששונה ממנו משמעותית.
לכשתהלך בנתיב זה - אליו צריך להתרגל - תישמט כנראה הקרקע מתחת לרוב שאלותיך.

questions.title_en: Each section of the Shemonei Esrei representing a section in the Beis HaMikdosh
questions.question:
I heard in the name of Rav Glatstein that the morning-tefillos represent certain areas in the Beis HaMikdosh. For example:

  • All the tefilos that precede Birchas Hashachar, represents the Ezras Nashim (The Women's Courtyard), for example "yigdal".

  • Birchas Hashachar consists of 15 brachos. Why 15? Because to get from the Ezras Nashim to the area of the Ezras Yisroel, there are exactly 15 steps. So each bracha of the Birchas Hashachar, represents one step.

  • Parshas HaTamid (the Korbonos-section of shacharis (morning prayer) is read during shacharis. Korbonos represent the mizbeach.

  • So, now we are at the mizbeach, when reciting the Parshas HaTamid. But we need to go to the Heichal - the area of the Holy of Holies. You'll need to climb 12 steps. The platform of the ulam has 13 steps - corresponding to the "Thirteen Principles of Torah Exegesis"

@Avishai Tebeka got the English translation of what I was looking for, but does anyone know if this can also be found in the original Hebrew-version?

answers.text: Can be found in sefer Iyun Tefilla by Rav Shimon Schwab from page xxx-xxxiii, sorry if formatting or pictures don't work it's my first time posting pictures :)

In addition to what Avishai Tebeka wrote, the original can be found in the sefer Iyun Tefillah by Rav Shimon Schwab (פתיחה, p. 22):

ולאור הקדמה זו, כשנתבונן בסדר תפלת שחרית שתקנו חכמים, נראה שמבנה התפלה דומה לסדר הבנין של הבית המקדש, וכאילו המתפלל עולה בקודש דרך שערי העזרה וההיכל עד התקרבו לפני ולפנים להתייחד עם קונו

And in light of this introduction, when we reflect on the order of the Shacharis prayer established by the sages, it appears that the structure of the prayer is similar to the order of the building of the Temple, as if the worshipper ascends in sanctity through the gates of the courtyard and the sanctuary until approaching the innermost sanctum to commune with his Maker.

questions.question:
למה אי אפשר לאכול במקום שיש רק תעודת כשרות של אותה העיר? 

ב"ה 
שלום וברכה 
כשרות ניתנת על פי החוק על ידי רבנות מקומית למה שמיוצר בארץ ועל ידי הרבנות הראשית למה שמיוצר בחו"ל.
קיימת כשרות רגילה וכשרות מהדרין. כשרויות של בדצי"ם אפשרית על פי החוק רק עם כבר יש כשרות של רבנות. לא תמיד עושים לפי החוק.
בברכה
הרב חגי פנחס בר-גיורא

questions.title_en: Wearing a Bendel Minhag Chabad
questions.question:
Minhag Chabad is to wear a Gartel (generally called a Bendel) all the time under the shirt. This accomplishes 2 things:

  1. Separates the heart and Erva for davening etc.

  2. Keeps the Tzitzis in place so that they are an Amoh wide the entire time.

After marriage, the Minhag is to continue wearing the Bendel but to wear a Gartel over the jacket when davening or performing various Mitzvos.

If one continues to wear the Bendel, why does one need a Gartel?

(I'm not asking why if one has a Gartel then by marriage why do they continue wearing a bendel, because it continues to hold the Tzitzis in place so that would make sense)

I have heard a nice explanation that just like a Sefer Torah if its kosher then belt is on the inside but if it's passul then the belt goes on the outside. So a bachur who is involved in Torah etc. is "kosher" but a married man has a home a wife and kids and therefore is less involved he is "passul". But this is a nice thought, not a halchic reason.

שלום וברכה!
יש את קלפי המשחק הרגילים (עם הסמלים של הלב. עלה. תילתן ומעויין) ומישהו אמר לי שאסור לשחק איתם כי זה סמלים של טומאה. (משחק מלחמה או ספיד. לא הימורים) אשמח לדעת אם באמת יש בזה בעיה. תודה רבה

אין כל בעיה.

האם השם קמה טוב לבת? (בעה יהיה גם שם שני, כנראה לאה) 

אם הכוונה לקמה של דגן כשהוא בשיא פריחתו זהו שם טוב.
אבל בסוגריים אני מוסיף שחברות עלולות לצחוק עליה ולומר היא קמה והיא נפלה וכדומה, וזה יכול להציק לה ח"ו אז כדאי להביא גם את זה בחשבון.

כבוד הרב, מברכים "שנהיה תמיד בצד הנותן". הרי ידוע שכדי לתת צריך גם לקבל. האם נכון לאמר שעצם זה שאני מזכה מישהו במצוות הנותן, זה מזכה אותי במצווה במעלה גבוהה יותר. שאלה זה מדירה שינה מעייני כי לאחרונה אני מסכים לאחר לחצים רבים מאימי לקבל תשורה אבל אני עושה זאת רק היות ואני מזכה אותה במצוות הנותן.

כשאדם מקבל וכוונתו לשמח את הנותן, זה נחשב מבחינה רוחנית שהוא נותן ולא מקבל. במיוחד להורים זה  מאוד משמח אותם כשבנם מקבל מהם ולכן אין להימנע מזה.

questions.title_en: Source for minhag to not eat whole hard boiled eggs?
questions.question:
I know people (including myself) who don't eat whole hard-boiled eggs, i.e. after boiling the egg they cut the egg in half or quarters and then eat it. The reason I heard was that eating an egg whole represents minhag aveilut, since aveilim eat whole hard-boiled eggs. Is there a source for this minhag?

I have had this question for many years already, I searched many sefarim and have found nothing, and asked many people but have not got an answer, I would really happy if someone knows the answer :)

questions.title_en: May Jews remove nose hair or eyelashes during Sefirat Ha’Omer
questions.question: According to Halacha, may Jews remove nose hair or eyelashes during Sefirat Ha’Omer, or no, do the semi mourning restrictions during this time not prohibit nose hair or eyelash removal? Or is this question a Machloket amongst the Poskim?

answers.text:
Refer to this respons at Dinonline.org:

Essentially the minhag not to cut hair applies to all hair of the body and not only to facial hair. However it is permitted for a woman to tweeze unsightly hair such as from her eyebrows nose ears, as this is not considered taking a haircut. (In general for a man, it is not permitted even not during sefira because of lo tilbash). A married woman may shave her legs if not shaving them will bother her husband.

Sources: O:CH 551-12, Aruch Hashulchan ibid 31, Kovetz Halachos (Sefira) 10-1,2, Hilchos Chag Bchag (Sefiras Haomer) 7-14 ftnt. 55, M:B 79, Y:D 182-1.

questions.title_en: What is Ramban's true opinion regarding the scope of hashgachah pratis?
questions.question:
Ramban seemingly contradicts himself regarding this subject.

In Bereishis 18:19 (and Iyov 36:7) he says explicitly that only the righteous are under total divine protection; others, which comprise the majority of people, are left to the vagaries of nature.

ירמוז כי ידיעת השם שהיא השגחתו בעולם השפל היא לשמור הכללים, וגם בני האדם מונחים בו למקרים עד בא עת פקודתם, אבל בחסידיו ישים אליו לבו לדעת אותו בפרט, להיות שמירתו דבוקה בו תמיד, לא תפרד הידיעה והזכירה ממנו כלל, כטעם: לא יגרע מצדיק עינו (איוב ל"ו:ז'). ובאו מזה פסוקים רבים, כדכתיב: הנה עין י"י אל יראיו (תהלים ל"ג:י"ח) וזולת זה.

He is thus alluding that G-d's knowledge, which is synonymous with His Providence in the lower world, is to guard the species, and even the children of men are subject despite it to the circumstantial evil occurrences until the time of their visitation comes. But as regards His pious, He directs His Providence to know each one individually so that His watch constantly attaches to him, His knowledge and remembrance of him never departs, as it says: He withdraweth not His eyes from the righteous.⁠ There are many verses on this theme, as it is written, Behold, the eye of the Eternal is toward them that fear Him,⁠ and other verses besides.

Whereas in Shemos 13:16 Ramban is quite forceful that nature is merely a smokescreen for the total divine micromanagement of everyone.

ומן הנסים הגדולים המפורסמים, אדם מודה בנסים הנסתרים שהם יסוד התורה כלה, שאין לאדם חלק בתורת משה רבינו עד שיאמין שכל דברינו ומקרינו כולם נסים אין בהם טבע ומנהגו של עולם, בין ברבים בין ביחיד, אלא אם יעשה המצות יצליחנו שכרו, ואם יעבר עליהן יכריתנו עונשו הגדול בגזרת עליון כאשר הזכרתי כבר

Through the great open miracles, one comes to admit the hidden miracles which constitute the foundation of the whole Torah, for no one can have a part in the Torah of Moses our teacher unless he believes that all our words and our events, [as dictated in the Torah], are miraculous in scope, there being no natural or customary way of the world in them, whether affecting the public or the individual. Instead, if a person observes the commandments, His reward will bring him success, and if he violates them, His punishment will cause his extinction. It is all by decree of the Most High, as I have already mentioned.

How to reconcile?

answers.text: In the second, he called the general miracles hidden. i.e., the difference is that with the righteous it is not hidden.

questions.title_en: What is the halacha on going barefoot outdoors (e.g., swimming on a beach or a "grounding" walk for health and getting sunlight in the morning)?
questions.question:
Here's some context for my question: I like going for morning walks in my bare feet through the grass or in the sand. In addition to getting a healthy amount of sunlight, many medical and biological professionals believe that this has a positive affect called 'grounding' on the body, which has many health benefits that I won't rabbit trail into in this post.

I was recently listening to a teaching while working out in the morning, and the Rabbi mentioned something negative about being barefoot that made me question my morning practice.

Since hearing this, I began researching the subject, and have found a few answers, but none of them answered my question within the intended context that I'm searching for.

I'm curious if there are any specific parameters to the subject of being barefoot, both indoors and outdoors, but especially outdoors.

Certain nuanced, context-related questions arise for me on this topic, such as, "If going barefoot is always bad, does that mean we should also swim with water shoes?"

As a note, I do not think biological indicators or health-related measurements are always a proper lens for considering mitzvot or halachah and their spiritual consequences.

For example, many modern doctors and other medical professionals recommend bacon for brain health, shellfish for joint health, and frequently prescribe medications containing pork. To me, "health benefits" can be just another form of temptation.

One must ask themselves, "Do I value the physical benefits of this thing, or obedience to HaShem, regardless of benefits?" Obedience itself IS the benefit, and if it's the only one, it's a blessing.

This said, I do like these morning walks. Is it proper to continue taking them barefoot, or should I throw on some shoes? If swimming on the beach or anywhere outdoors, what then? Others may be able to think of other instances in which the nuances of halachah on going barefoot become relevant, but I think you get the gist, by now.

Thank you in advance for any insights! I am excited to learn (and will keep my shoes on, in the meantime, just in case lol).

History and sources are greatly appreciated.

UPDATE: I just learned that there are special "grounding shoes" created to provide the same health-related benefits. Interestingly enough, most of them are mode of leather or at least have leather soles.

From my very limited knowledge of shoe fashion throughout history, leather shoes were frequently worn during the time periods of most of the people we read about in the scriptures. Maybe they were benefiting from grounding all along! Lol

This still wouldn't answer my question, however, especially about swimming outdoors.

answers.text:
Mishna Brura (OC 2:14) writes

Our Sages have taught that a person should sell everything he owns in order to buy shoes for his feet. In the Arab countries where they normally walk barefoot, it is permitted. [...]

The Dirshu MB edition brings 3 reasons for not walking barefoot

  • out of tzniut (Chofetz Chaim)
  • because of the cold (Maharsha)
  • because there is no bigger shame than to walk barefoot in the market (Rashi)

It is very possible that, where it is customary to walk barefoot in the sand, such as at the beach, it would be permitted. Actually MB 4:53 writes exactly this

[...] Machatzit Hashekel wrote that it depends on the custom of the place, if it's the way of people there to have those parts exposed.

Last, note MB 301:62 writes than even then on Shabbat and Yom Tov one should wear shoes.

Of course, consult your rabbi before implementing anything you learn here.

questions.title_en: Can you do an Aveira when someone is taking away all of your money, and what do poskim say on the matter
questions.question: The Pasuk says that we should live by the Mitzvos, which teaches us that we can do an Aveira to save our, or someone else's life. The Midrash says that people who have nothing are like dead people, so maybe you would be able to do an aveira if someone is robbing you of all your money if you do not do it.

answers.text:
The halacha is one must give up all his money not to do an aveirah. (Obviously this assumes no other workaround or option.)

As a general rule, when we say one thing is "like" another thing, that means there is a comparison in at least one aspect, nothing more. If the two things were identical, they would be the same, not merely "alike".

questions.title_en: Is it true there was a sage on his death bed and said I wish I used up all my money?
questions.question:
BH

Is it true that there was a sage on his death bed who said I wish I used up all my money?

answers.text:
Reish Lakish, in Gittin 47a:

כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ שְׁבַק קַבָּא דְמוֹרִיקָא, קְרָא אַנַּפְשֵׁיהּ: ״וְעָזְבוּ לַאֲחֵרִים חֵילָם״

When he passed away, he left a kav of saffron. He applied to himself the verse (Tehillin 49:11), "They leave their wealth to others."

Maharsha ad loc. cites in this connection Eruvin 54a, that "it is the way of fools" to want to make sure to leave an inheritance, so Reish Lakish regretted that he was doing so.

Ein Eliyahu ad loc. observes that there are other places in the Gemara where leaving an inheritance is seen as a positive thing to do. He notes that since Reish Lakish himself had been a bandit earlier in life (Bava Metzia 84a), he might have been particularly worried that his children might follow in the same path and misuse their legacy. Although he instead suggests that Reish Lakish figured that all of his possessions ought to go towards paying back his erstwhile victims (or, if they couldn't be traced, using the funds for public-works projects).

The Chofetz Chaim (cited here) offers yet another reason: the time he spent earning the money to buy that kav of saffron was, in retrospect, wasted.

questions.title_en: Why didn't G-d make us resistant to pain or blows?
questions.question: Why didn't G-d make us resistant to pain or blows? Keep in mind that prior to the creation of human beings, G-d made angels, who do not suffer from pain or the possibility of losing their physical integrity, since they are spirits. Why, instead of making something of higher quality, did G-d grade creation downwards?

answers.text:
This is a great question!

The simplest answer is that pain was a curse that Adam and Chava brought upon themselves and their progeny by the chet. See Bereshit 3.

A practical answer is that they came down into a world of death. In such a world, pain is a blessing in disguise because it helps us stay alive (see Joel K's comment).

However, you hit the nail on the head when you generalized the question:

"Why, instead of making something of higher quality, did G-d grade creation downwards?"

This is part of the purpose of creation: Hashem's ta'avah is to dwell in the lowest world, and this is the lowest world. A world where there is pain and death, as well as joy and life.

For a quick explanation why, consider that unless it is the lowest world, Hashem Himself is not manifest. In higher realms, where He is more revealed, any being is overwhelmed by the lofty qualities of Hashem, such as His Holiness, etc. In this lowest world, Hashem is able to truly dwell, Himself. His Essence can become revealed only here, in a world where beings are not so overwhelmed by Him, and can therefore serve Him with the service of a simple servant.

This is covered extensively in Chassidut. See Maamar Velakachtem Lechem, 5661; Maamarim Yom Tov shel Rosh HaShanah 5666, p. 438; Likkutei Sichot, Vol. 12, p. 73ff.; Vol. 14 p. 123; Vol 15 p. 243ff, Vayeitzei III and the full Maamar Veshavti BeShalom; plus many many other places.

questions.title_he: האם במלחמת גוג ומגוג כל הגויים יבואו לישראל?
questions.question:
יש כמות בלתי מבוטלת של גוים שכופרים בכל הדתות, ולא תהיה להם סיבה רציונלית לבוא לארץ ישראל אפילו לא לטייל.
בדרך כלל כל רב שמדבר על גוג ומגוג אומר ששבעים (ה)אומות יבואו להילחם בארץ ישראל.. אז האם באמת במלחמת גוג ומגוג כל הגויים יבואו לישראל?.


אין כל ידיעה מוחלטת בדברים אלה, ולא נדע עד שיהיו. 
כל האומר אחרת - לכל היותר משער, מפרש, דן וכו', ותו לא. 
האומר דברים בבטחון מוחלט, כביכול יודע מה שיהיה - אינו אמין. 
וכבר אמרו חז"ל (סנהדרין צז ע"ב): "אמר רבי שמואל בר נחמני אמר רבי יונתן: תיפח עצמן של מחשבי קיצין", 
וכן הורה הרמב"ם בפירוש המשנה לפרק חלק: "והיסוד השנים עשר ימות המשיח, והוא להאמין ולאמת שיבא ואין לומר שנתאחר אם יתמהמה חכה לו, ואין לקבוע לו זמן, ולא לפרש את המקראות כדי להוציא מהן זמן בואו, אמרו חכמים תפוח דעתן של מחשבי קצין".  וכן שנה בהלכות מלכים ומלחמות פי"ב ה"ב: "יראה מפשוטן של דברי הנביאים, שבתחילת ימות המשיח תהיה מלחמת גוג ומגוג, ושקודם מלחמת גוג ומגוג יעמוד נביא לישר ישראל ולהכין לבם, שנאמר הנה אנכי שולח לכם את אליה וגו', ואינו בא לא לטמא הטהור, ולא לטהר הטמא, ולא לפסול אנשים שהם בחזקת כשרות, ולא להכשיר מי שהוחזקו פסולין, אלא לשום שלום בעולם, שנאמר והשיב לב אבות על בנים, ויש מן החכמים שאומרים שקודם ביאת המשיח יבא אליהו, וכל אלו הדברים וכיוצא בהן לא ידע אדם איך יהיו עד שיהיו, שדברים סתומין הן אצל הנביאים, גם החכמים אין להם קבלה בדברים אלו, אלא לפי הכרע הפסוקים, ולפיכך יש להם מחלוקת בדברים אלו, ועל כל פנים אין סדור הויית דברים אלו ולא דקדוקיהן עיקר בדת, ולעולם לא יתעסק אדם בדברי ההגדות, ולא יאריך במדרשות האמורים בענינים אלו וכיוצא בהן, ולא ישימם עיקר, שאין מביאין לא לידי יראה ולא לידי אהבה, וכן לא יחשב הקצין, אמרו חכמים תפח רוחם של מחשבי הקצים, אלא יחכה ויאמין בכלל הדבר כמו שבארנו". וכך עוד רבים.

questions.title_en: Recording Shmonah Esrei
questions.question:
Now is the period around Pesach in which there are two new additions to the Amida:

  1. Morid Hatal (or the omission of Geshem)

  2. V'sen Bracha

The Halacha is, that if one is davening and isn't sure whether he made those additions to Shmonah Esrei, he must go back if it's in the first 30 days because he probably made a mistake and said it the way he's said it since Sukkot.

(This is a general summary. More details including which addition and how long after you realized you made the mistake, may change the Halacha)

If one has the possibility of recording his Shmonah Esrei eg. He isn't davening with a minyan, would it be preferable and he would be able to listen back during the Amida and check what he said and maybe even during the 30 day period he wouldn't have to repeat the amida if he actually said it right?

This would entail him firstly to daven loud enough to record what he's saying and secondly, stopping during the Amida to listen on his recording device what he said.

Or is it preferred that he go back to the begining with it possibly being a bracha levatala?

questions.title_en: Was there a "before" to creation from a Kabbalistic perspective?
questions.question:
In briefly reading the Sefir Yetzirah, it has this picture of creation:

It symbolizes the process whereby the infinite engraved, creating a void, which was then filled with possibility in essence, and that was the beginning of creation.

What came before? Is it an infinite cycle of some sort? If so, how does it transition from one phase to the next?

I also briefly read about the Buddhist cycle of creation, whereby my understanding was essentially this:

The universe is in constant flow from pain -> pleasure, and when it reaches ultimate pleasure, the ultimate pleasure is to grow through the pain -> pleasure process again, so the cycle starts over. The goal though is not pleasure or pain, it is to escape the cycle. It is to be like a good swimmer in a river, staying afloat in one spot, being a constant in an ever-changing environment. The goal is in the middle, peace, which is a constant, a balance between the two poles. The “flow” from pain -> pleasure is a chaotic up/down movement, so it’s not a straight line. It is like the mixing ocean, where things move up and down in a seemingly random fashion, based on their actions and sin.

In this sense, there is no beginning and end to creation from that perspective. But then I imagine the physical world, which seems to have been evolving toward more perfection, and so seems to be trending toward the upward direction. The Buddhist perspective can be seen like this too, which would mean at some point it reaches pure perfection, and either starts over from scratch, or reverses like a pendulum. I have no idea yet.

So from the perspective of Kabbalah, what happens before creation, way before creation. And what happens before that? And before that? Is it a cycle of some sort as well?

answers.text:
No, there is no cycle. Buddhist thought is incorrect. There is only one being without beginning (בְּלִי רֵאשִׁית), and that is Hashem Himself. Even His Infinite light is called אור אין סוף, "Light without end", but not without beginning. It begins from His Essence and Being1.

Stating that the world is somehow in some infinite cycle is actually a heretical thought according to Torah, because the Zohar clearly states that Hashem is not a creator in essence (that's infinitely beneath Him)2; He created the universe out of absolute nothingness. Not just from zero raw materials, but absolute zero - not even potential, not even out of some logical argument3.

He created the world with a purpose and a plan, and it will be accomplished, and in one go (although there is what to discuss about a finite number of worlds that came before this4). The purpose and the plan is for the creation to become one with Him, and this will be forever (and not restart, chas veshalom)5.

1. Derech Mitzvotecha He'Emanut Elokut Ch. 5
2. Sourced in Maamer of 1st night Shavuot 5668; Hemshech Teerav pp. 135, 1144
3. E.g. Bereshit Rabba 1:4; Ramban on Bereshit 1:1; Likutei Torah Bamidbar 14:24. See this answer.
4. E.g Chagiga 13b-14a; Bereshit Rabba 3:7; Zohar Bereshit 25a. See this answer.
5. Maamer Veyadata 5657. See this answer.

B"H

"What came before"

Before what? Prior to that you said:

"the process whereby the infinite engraved, creating a void, which was then filled with possibility in essence, and that was the beginning of creation."

This concept of the engraving, "glif glifu bitihiru olah", is referring to after the tzimtzim. Before the tzimtzim, there was the Ohr Ein Sof. Before the Ohr Ein Sof, there was the Etzem Haoyr (the essence of the (infinite) light)

Before the essence there were 2 prior levels:

The maor -- luminary The yecholes -- the 'ability ' Hashem has to create (or not create)

This 'ability', as mentioned, has two (prior) stages:

The ability to not "shine" the light, and thus create eventually (with the light), and instead just become elevated away from existence, into the Essence, and

The ability to "shine" and become revealed

And beyond those two levels -- the essence of the ability, before it's divided into two potential aspects, but just united in the Essence, the Atzmus (Awtsmoos).

Before the ability, there is just the Awtsmoos itself, the Essence of the Creator, the necessary existence, the 'Truth of His Being' (Rambam hilchos yesodei hatorah chapter 1), beyond any and everything.

The Awtsmoos can be revealed in three "levels" of Revelation, similar to chesed, gevurah and tiferes, but on a much more sublime level:

Either the Awtsmoos can be revealed openly in everything directly, in which case even little babies know that there is a G-d found everywhere. This is the 'revelation' of the Awtsmoos, and the original "source" of the idea of the "ability" to shine. At this level, we refer to the Awtsmoos in the second person, "blessed are you", since it's as of we are looking directly at him and facing Him.

Another 'level' in how the singular Awtsmoos can be revealed, is in a way of concealment. This refers to Joe the Awtsmoos is "elevated", so to speak, into it's own Essence, and away from the potential for existence. Paradoxically, this concealment is actually the source for Creation, because creation exists through the Awtsmoos being hidden in the world, through the tzimtzim

(Even though the tzimtzim is only in the light but not even in the luminary, and for sure not in the Awtsmoos, but this level is the ultimate "source" for the idea of the concealment at all)

This level is referred to in the third person, when we say "blessed is He", since He is hidden, like when one refers to someone who's "over there" and so to speak not "here" (even though He's also here as He is everywhere, but at this level He is concealed). This is the source for the ability not to shine. The ability to be concealed.

Then the third level is the Essential Name, the name of Havaya, which is the name of the Essence, that, so to speak, "contains" the Essence. This is the combination of revelation and concealment.

Source: Sefer HaMaamarim meluket, d"H vichazakta.

אתה הוא הוי' לבדך את עשית את השמים גו' ואתה מחי' את כולם, שהם ג' מדריגות13. אתה הוא הוי' לבדך קאי על אוא"ס שלפני הצמצום [ומפרט בזה ג' ענינים, אתה הוא והוי'. אתה הוא עצמות המאור, ואומר על זה אתה לשון נוכח, כי העצמות הוא בכל מקום בהתגלות14, דשם שמים שגור בפי כל. הוא והוי' הם ב' מדריגות בהאור, עצם האור (הוא), והתפשטות האור (הוי'), כמבואר בהמאמר. ואומר על זה לבדך, שאין כאן דבר זולת העצמות, כי כללות האור שלפני הצמצום, גם האור השייך לעולמות (הוי'), הוא כלול בעצמותו ואינו בבחי' מציאות15]. את עשית את השמים גו' הוא האור כמו שנעשה מקור להתהוות העולמות. ולכן כתיב את עשית, את חסר ה', כי האור, גם האור השייך לעולמות (הוי'), כמו שהוא לפני הצמצום, אינו בערך להיות מקור לעולמות, ובכדי שיהי' מקור לעולמות הוא ע"י הצמצום, שנתעלם כל האור ונמשך רק קו קצר ומצומצם. וזהו את עשית את השמים גו' את חסר ה', דזה שהאור נעשה מקור לעולמות (עשית את השמים גו') הוא ע"י שנחסר ונתמעט (את חסר ה'). ואתה מחי' את כולם הוא הקו שעל ידו נמשך חיות לעולמות, לאחרי שנתהוו. והיינו, שבהקו שני ענינים, שהוא קו קצר ומצומצם, ומצד זה הוא מהוה את העולמות (מציאות העולמות), ושהמשכתו היא מהאור שלפני הצמצום, ומצד זה הוא ממשיך חיות בעולמות (גילוי אלקות)16. וזהו שאתה זה (ואתה מחי' את כולם) הוא מלא ה' כמו אתה הראשון (אתה הוא הוי' לבדך), כי ענין זה שבהקו שהוא מחי' את כולם, הוא מצד זה שנמשך בו גילוי האור שלפני הצמצום.

questions.title_en: Does G-d experience pain?
questions.question:
I am trying to think through how He could create the universe, filled with pleasure and pain (heaven and hell), and yet not experience all of it together? In His infinite oneness, permeating all of creation, He would seemingly have to empathize with His creation, and therefore feel pain, and yet at the same time be beyond pain and pleasure somehow. But if the infinite oneness is perfected, or in "perfect harmony and balance", wouldn't that mean He only experiences either pure pleasure or pure peace, and so be located on one side of the pain-peace-pleasure spectrum? Or would it mean He experiences the full spectrum at once, and therefore knows complete pain and complete pleasure, or something like that?

What is the Jewish / Kabbalah perspective on this?

answers.text:
The Mishnah (Sanhedrin 6:5), as printed, seems to indicate that God does participate in human pain:

אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר, בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָדָם מִצְטַעֵר, שְׁכִינָה מַה הַלָּשׁוֹן אוֹמֶרֶת כִּבְיָכוֹל, קַלַּנִי מֵרֹאשִׁי, קַלַּנִי מִזְּרוֹעִי. אִם כֵּן הַמָּקוֹם מִצְטַעֵר עַל דָּמָם שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים שֶׁנִּשְׁפַּךְ, קַל וָחֹמֶר עַל דָּמָם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים.

Rabbi Meir said: The phrase “for he that is hung is a curse [kilelat] of God” should be understood as follows: When a man suffers in the wake of his sin, what expression does the Divine Presence use? I am distressed [kallani] about My head, I am distressed about My arm, meaning, I, too, suffer when the wicked are punished. From here it is derived: If God suffers such distress over the blood of the wicked that is spilled, even though they justly deserved their punishment, it can be inferred a fortiori that He suffers distress over the blood of the righteous.

However, if one looks in Rambam's commentary one will see that he possessed a different text of the Mishnah (which omits שכינה) which does away with such a connotation. It jives well with Rambam's notion of a transcendent God.

(מה הלשון אומרת כלומר איזה דבר הוא מנהג בני אדם לומר כשהוא רוצה לענות מי שמצטער בצערו אין הנאה בזה המעשה ולא בהנחתו והדברים שהיו אומרים בימי ר"מ קלני מראשי קלני מזרועי כך אמר הכתוב שבמיתת זה החוטא יש חורבן המציאות ולהניח אותו בחיים אין טוב ואם זה אומר במחויב מיתה כ"ש מי שנהרג נקי)

Hello Lance and welcome to Mi Yodeya.

Your instinct and reason about this subject are aimed in the right direction.

The general rule from the traditional Jewish viewpoint (including Kabbalah) is that G-d is one. This implies consequentially that nothing from the created universe which we experience and perceive through our senses is separate and apart from G-d.

But like you raise in your question, doesn't that mean that in terms of how we understand and experience the universe, that there must be some kind of deficiency with G-d if G-d is not lacking what we experience?

To this, we have a teaching from Elijah the Prophet, who explains to us in regard to G-d, that G-d's thoughts (and consequentially G-d's emotions, feelings, etc., which arise from intellect according to the order implanted and imbued throughout all of creation by the Creator) are not like our thoughts. The Prophet uses similar Hebrew words sharing a common word root, which means they have a common meaning but are categorically different (like for example חכים ולא בחכמה ידיעא, מבין ולא בבינה ידיעא, Wise and not with known Wisdom, Understanding and not with known understanding), to distinguish our experience from G-d.

You know when people say "you don't have to let them hurt you, it's your choice". This is because your essential self is unaffectable - you are a free being. Only you can affect yourself. This is part of the philosophy of essence, which is a philosophy that is not controversial either among the philosophers of Chakira, or the Kabbalists, or the Chassidim who tried to resolve both camps into a unified teaching.

If a person is a man of strength by Torah standards, then he is able to retain this "unaffected" state, and decide, using his own leadership and initiative, based on his own decision, how to feel about anything and everything (and if he is Kadosh, it will be in line with Torah always). As Ben Zoma states in Avot 4:1:

Who is strong? He who conquers his inclination, as it is said: “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city” (Mishlei 16:32)

The Rambam states in the Moreh that attributing human emotions, and things like pain and pleasure to Hashem is nonsensical. Human feelings are reactive, instinctive creations that affect someone, and are also very lowly - definitely non-applicable to Hashem. Hashem's knowledge of our pain, however, is His self knowledge. All is indeed one with Him, like you state, and He knows it with a perfect knowledge (Mishneh Torah). This perfect knowledge is also not something we can describe as "Hashem experiencing" either, according to Rambam. "Experiencing" is a human way of looking at things (too lowly for Hashem, and also implies He is being affected).

The Kabbalist the Maharal takes this a step further in Gevurot Hashem, and states that even knowledge is not "His Essence". Similar to the Moreh, claiming that Hashem "knows" in any way that we can conceive or express is incorrect, and the sublime truth of the matter is level upon level of sublime loftiness, removed from our understanding or grasp. Knowledge, as we know it, is just a creation to Hashem, as distant from His Essence as a stone or physical action is.

The Ramak (teacher of the Arizal) resolves this in Pardes Rimonim by saying that both are correct (and built upon by the Tzemach Tzedek in Derech Mitzvotecha). The Rambam, when he talks about Hashem being the Knower, the Knowledge and the Known, in a great oneness of knowledge that is beyond our comprehension and our ability to utter or hear, is referring to the Sefirot of Atzilut. From Hashem's point of view, these are indeed as lowly as pebbles, but from our point of view, loftier than the mind can comprehend, infinite and ineffable.

Despite that, they are created from Godliness, and He identifies with them. So when we say Hashem knows, it is appropriate to say He knows with His Chochma. We can therefore say that what He knows can indeed be pain. It can be the pain of humanity, or it can be pain relevant to the Sefirot of Atzilut themselves. The former is just a mashal of a mashal of the latter, and the latter is a tzimtzum of true Godliness.

ובפרט מצד מקור נשמותינו

And specifically, [how much more so does the pain we share in our unified souls be felt] by the Source of our souls (Derech Mitzvotecha Isur Sinat Yisrael, Mitzvat Ahavat Yisrael 1:1)

Another source is in Tomer Devorah, by the Ramak, by the fourth Midda of Rachamim:

והינו לשארית נחלתו לשון שאר בשר וסוף סוף הם נחלתו. ומה אמר, אם אענישם הרי הכאב עלי כדכתיב (ישעיה סג, ט) בכל צרתם לו צר.

This, too, is the meaning of the words "the she'erit [remnant] of His heritage," implying she'er basar, a blood relationship. In the final analysis, the children of Israel are God's inheritance. Says the Holy One, Blessed be He: "If I punish them, the pain is Mine!", as it is written, "In all their trouble, He is afflicted..." (Yeshayahu 63:9).

The Ramak goes on to prove that the pain is His, and not limited to a particular Sefira or level of the Seder Hishtalshelus (the spiritual cosmos, including His revelations within it).

Now to finish where we started. He can also choose whether on not to actually be hurt or not. We can't affect Him, He is Mighty. But don't limit Hashem, He is beyond limit (even beyond the limit of being beyond limit! See Maamarim Yom Tov shel Rosh HaShana 5666 p. 167). Woe unto the person who does something and Hashem decides to let it hurt Him, because it is a true contradiction to His Essence that He cannot abide by! Generally, it seems that what He lets hurt Him, because it is a perfection to do so, is when He doesn't have us, because we sinned, or abandoned Him. We are His afterall, so this is the biggest violation of His Essence.

questions.question:
האם פרשת שקלים מדאוריתא או מדרבנן?

שלום וברכה,
קריאת פרשת שקלים אינה מהתורה אלא היא תקנת חכמים. הטעם שקורים פרשת שקלים הוא לזכר מצות מחצית השקל, שבזמן המקדש בחודש אדר היו מכריזים בכל ערי ישראל שיביאו את מחצית השקל עבור קרבנות המקדש (כמבואר במסכת שקלים פרק א משנה א). הטעם שהיו מכריזים על השקלים מחודש אדר הוא משום שמחודש ניסן היה צריך להביא את קרבנות התמידים והמוספים משקלים מהתרומה החדשה. לכן תיקנו לקרוא את פרשת שקלים בחודש אדר (משנה ברורה תרפה ס"ק א-ב). 


הרחבה:
עוד מובא בגמרא (מגילה יג:): "אמר ריש לקיש: גלוי וידוע לפני מי שאמר והיה העולם שעתיד המן לשקול שקלים על ישראל, לפיכך הקדים שקליהן לשקליו. והיינו דתנן: באחד באדר משמיעין על השקלים ועל הכלאים".

שלום וברכה,
בהמשך לשאלתי אסביר למה התכוונתי:

האם לא לספר משהו מסוים לפלוני, שווה ערך ללשקר לו מבחינת היהדות?
כלומר אני יכול להגיד לו משהו שהוא רוצה לדעת, ואני לא אומר לו אותו. האם זה שווה ערך לשקר?

אם אתה לא מספר זה לא שקר. שקר זה לומר דבר שאינו נכון.
אבל, לפעמים זה לא בסדר לא לומר לו. למשל, אתה רואה אדם שהולך לסגור עסקה עם אדם שאתה יודע שיש סבירות גדולה שירמה אותו, אתה צריך לספר לו כדי שיבדוק היטב. או מישהי שהולכת להתחתן ואתה יודע שלבחור או לבחורה יש בעיה מסויימת אתה צריך לספר כדי שיבדקו אם זה מתאים. כמובן שיש לעשות את זה בזהירות וברגישות המתאימה.

האם כותנה הוא פשתן לענין איסור שעטנז?

כותנה זה לא פשתן. הם שני סוגי צמחים אחרים.

האם כותנה היא פשתן לעניין שעטנז?.

ב"ה 
שלום וברכה 
כותנה של היום היא לא פשתן.
בברכה הרב חגי פנחס בר-גיורא

questions.title_en: Source for quote from Hagaon Hagadol Rabbi Mordechai Gifter T'zl
questions.question:
"These days, bachurim are learning more and more about less and less. Eventually they will know everything about nothing".

Where is the source that he said this, and what did he mean?

I saw this in a meme, and the only further information on it is that it is captioned "someone requested something from Hagaon..."

answers.text:
The quote (“getting to know more and more about less and less”) is also well known from secular sources. I have personally heard it many times and first heard it well over 25 years ago.

Its history is investigated here

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2017/10/25/more/?amp=1

With this conclusion:

In conclusion, an early fragment was attributed to an unnamed distinguished Scottish person in 1911. Patrick Geddes received credit by 1915 and 1916 for presenting a warning about over specialization. More elaborate statements evolved during the ensuing decades.

questions.title_en: Are non-Jews who are converting to Judaism allowed to read the Talmud?
questions.question: A general question, I’ve been curious about. Are non-Jews who are converting to Judaism allowed to read the Talmud?

answers.text: Yes (you can) but with a huge caveat. Talmud isn't something to read like how one would read other religious writings, e.g. Christian Church Father writings or Islamic sunnah/tafseers, et cetera. To put it like this: if daf yomi (daily digests of Talmud tractates with additional discussions included) are something one (I tried this when I was still a Noahide, at the time not yet considering geirus... It's like sailing a boat into sea with no sail and no captain to consult) finds challenging, how much more is directly reading the Talmud (which doesn't have the discussions from the daf yomi)? From what the community I stayed with for Pesach told me, it's best to start with the parshas (weekly reading of the sections of Written Torah which mostly includes connections to Oral Torah, mileage may vary depending on your shul's rabbi). Jumping directly into Oral Torah will be tough for a geirus (who is still studying and immersing into following Torah). I also agree with what @mbloch has said about the distinction between reading and learning.

questions.title_en: Kosher Wine and Other Spirits
questions.question:
The Talmud gives two reasons for the prohibition of gentile wines:

  1. Gentile wines are at risk of use for Avodah Zarah.
  2. Gentile wines risk intermarriage: "And they issued the decree prohibiting their wine due to the fact that this leads to familiarity, and Jews will come to marry their daughters." (Avodah Zarah 36b)

So even if we are guaranteed on who is not idol worshipper has produced the wine, we are not permitted to drink it due to the risk of intermarriage. Halachipedia concurs :

"Muslims are not idol worshippers, so their wine and wine they touch is only prohibited from drinking, because of intermarriage. Rishonim and Acharonim unanimously voice this ruling."

So why aren't spirits and other intoxicants similarly prohibited? Are not the risks of "familiarity" just as present with vodka as with wine?

questions.title_en: Must people be informed they are terminally ill?
questions.question:
In Judaism, do doctors or other informed parties have a halachic obligation to tell a person he is terminally ill? Or to lie to him by telling him his affliction is treatable?

Of course, one can argue that hope is ever present, but I am talking only about communicating statistics based on the record, nothing more. One can also argue that a person has the right to know so he can prepare. Anything on the matter from our Sages?

questions.title_en: When did they start using the term ashkenazi?
questions.question: About what year was the term Ashkenazi first used? Was it first used only for German Jews or also for French Jews?

In the Gemara (Brachot 35b) Rabbi Shimon Bar Yochai famously says that the phrase "ואספת דגנך" from the Kriat Shma is describing a fallen state, when Am Israel is not being holy enough:

...when Israel performs God’s will, their work is performed by others, as it is stated: “And strangers will stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners will be your plowmen and your vinedressers” (Isaiah 61:5)When Israel does not perform God’s will, their work is performed by them themselves, as it is stated: “And you shall gather your grain.”

But in the original context the words "ואספת דגנך" are the very description of what happens when Israel does Hashems will, with all their heart and all their soul.

Why and how can Rabbi Shimon take this verse so much out of context?

answers.text:
Rabbi Shimon was of the opinion that the correct state of the world is where Jews and non Jews form a partnership similar to Yissachar and Zevulun, where the Jews sit and learn Torah and the non-Jews take responsibility for the physical world, including providing sustenance. See Yoma 3b, and Abba Chanan's statement in the name of Rav Elazar, for another source of this state the Jews can be in.

There is another state, where we have to both provide for ourselves and learn. This is the position of Rabbi Ishmael in your gemara. This is a lower state.

Why is this mentioned then, as a blessing in Shema? Well, perhaps the answer is this. The first paragraph of Shema is addressed to the Tzaddik, and we know this because it expects the Jew to love Hashem with all his me'od, his extreme.

The second paragraph of Shema is in reference to a Jew who is not a Tzaddik (and doesn't say "with all your extreme"). It even starts with "if you listen...".

So, the fact that there is even an "if" implies a lower state. It's not an evil state, but it's certainly lower. In that setting, we have to work and learn, and we will be blessed with success, if we listen.

This is based on Maamer Basi Legani 1951.

questions.title_he: Seeking recommendations for a set of טור ושולחן ערוך
questions.question:
I am seeking recommendations for a set of טור ושולחן ערוך. (A set “in progress” is worthwhile for consideration too — I mostly learn אורח חיים and יורה דעה so I’m not really needing a full set anyway other than that I’m mentally pre-programmed to want complete sets.)

For years I used an old set of טור and an old set of שולחן ערוך from my father, a”h, which were published in the early 1980s (or maybe late 1970s? I’m going off memory here). Both sets are sitting in storage back in the USA (I’m based in London, England now).

I’ve mostly been using digital text libraries for the last four years and am less up to date with published options. There are also not many well-stocked ספרים shops near me, so I’ve not had a chance to thumb through more recent options either.

I’d really like to get back into using actual published books — especially as my children are now getting closer to an age where I can learn with them on Shabbos.

My preferences are

  • clarity and corrected text are my primary considerations
  • I’d prefer fewer ראשי תיבות to make life easier but this is nice to have and not essential
  • Tzuras Hadaf is also nice enough but not a real consideration either way
  • I’m not concerned about pricing per se

In making recommendations, please include your reasoning. Thank you.

answers.text:
There are quite a few nice sets now available that are worth exploring.

  1. The Tzuras HaDaf - Tur Shulchan Aruch: Like the name suggests it is formatted and paginated with the traditional tzuras hadaf layout, but the text is nice and clear and a good primer in how to "read" the development of halacha.

  2. Tur Shulchan Aruch Habahir - Also very nice. Has lot of purchase options if you don't want to spend so much at once - i.e. you can buy just the Orach Chaim section as well as having multiple sizes.

  3. There is also the Tur Shulchan Aruch Hamaor, but I have not seen it properly to provide enough information on it.

questions.title_en: Can a Nidah do Kedushin?
questions.question:
Would a man giving a nidah a ring be an issue, since usually a husband can't hand their wife something when they are nidah?

Also, would both of them being isolated for nisuin be an issue?

answers.text:
The husband may put the ring on her finger if he does so without touching her skin, but some Rabbis might ask him to just put it in her hand.

After this all normal laws of Niddah are followed.

Yichud would not be allowed. There are discrete ways of handling this. One should speak to one's Rabbi.

There are other relevant details. All is discussed on this Yoatzot page.

There are ways of planning, or hormonal treatment options that many use to prevent this in the first place.

questions.question: It's forbidden to pray in front of a mirror, as it can appear like you're praying to your own reflection. What about standing on a mirrored floor (or some other reflective surface), where it can look like you're bowing to your reflection?

questions.title_en: Is Remilk dairy or pareve in Halacha
questions.question:
According to Halacha, is the animal free Remilk from Israel considered dairy for the purpose of seperating meat and dairy? Or no, since the milk is not from a live animal is it considered pareve and therefor isn’t prohibited from consumption with meat (as long as there is adequate showing it is not animal milk so there is no problem of Marit Ayin)? The reason I ask is because the article states

Founded in 2019, Remilk produces milk proteins via a yeast-based fermentation process that renders them “chemically identical” to those present in cow-produced milk and dairy products. The startup claims that the result is 100 percent similar to “real” milk.

answers.text:
Another animal-free 'milk' comes from Perfect Day. On their website they say,

Perfect Day’s non-animal whey protein is Kosher Certified. Like all food ingredients, our protein could end up in co-branded products that contain other components which are not Kosher, or Kosher but not Pareve. Please refer to product packaging to determine whether an individual product is Kosher or Kosher Pareve.

I cannot find which authority gives the hechsher but it seems that the pure product is considered pareve.

I have not been able to get a direct response from the OU on this topic (despite multiple attempts), perhaps because no uniform psak has been reached, and the topic is controversial/political.

As an additional datapoint, it seems the OU has given a pareve designation to the Bored Cow animal-free chocolate milk product that uses Perfect Day but an OU-D to Brave Robot Ice Cream.

questions.title_en: If a Jew accepts Shabbat early, is something new which came into existence then nolad
questions.question: According to Halacha, if a Jew accepts Shabbat early, is something new which comes into existence then (when it is still before when Shabbat would naturally start) considered nolad? Or no, since it is before when Shabbat would naturally start does nolad not apply?

answers.text:
Great question!

In no way am I paskening anything, please your LOR about this question:

The intro:

The major case where nolad is discussed is in Beitza 2a (and onwards) which discusses a case of a chicken laying an egg on yom tov (or shabbat), which the Gemera says is Nolad. This is paskened in Shulchan Aruch O.C. Siman 322:1. The Mishneh Berurah explains that it's nolad because Chachmim made a gzeira regarding Shabbat that falls after Yom Tov (or the opposite). In such a case, an egg laid on it is forbidden Medeoritah for consumption because any egg laid today was completed yesterday. Therefore, if we eat it, we find that it was prepared from Yom Tov for Shabbat. Also, if an egg is laid on a Yov Tov that falls on a Sunday, it is also forbidden Medeoritah to eat it, because it was certainly completed in the chicken's body the day before. Thus, when we eat it, we find that it was prepared from Shabbat to Yom Tov. Tosefet Shabbat is a machloket Rishonim if its Deoritah or Derabbanan. Rishonim who hold its deoritah are the Rif Yoma 2b, Rosh Yoma 8:8, Tosfoat Rosh Hashanah 9a, and the Ra’an Shabbat 15a etc, and from the Biur Halacha (O.C. Siman 261:2) it sounds like its deoritah since the majority of Rishonim hold that, including Shulchan Aruch (arguably). And Nolad (which is a category of muktzeh) is derabbanan.

Second intro:

In the Sefer Kovetz Yesodot Vechakirot page 1014 he writes about a chakirah regarding tosefet shabbat. One opinion holds that upon the early acceptance of Shabbat, it effectively begins in every sense. The other opinion suggests that Shabbat cannot truly start early; rather, Tosefet Shabbat implies that the individual takes on the prohibition of melachah before Shabbat officially begins. According to the ספר רץ כצבי on the topic גדרי תוספת שבת ויום טוב, he quotes the Taz in O.C. 291:6 who says, כתב בס"ח סי' רס"ט בליל שבת צריך שיהי' גמר הסעודה בלילה ורש"ל נהג שלא אכל בליל שבת עד הלילה. The Taz quotes the Sefer Chasidim who says that one must finish their shabbat meat at night (not during the day), and so did the Mahrashal. The Taz then disagrees and says, ול"נ כיון דתוס' מחול על הקדש הוא דאורייתא ע"כ יצא שפיר אפי' גמר קודם לילה. That Tosefet Shabbat is Deoritah (which is a machloket Rishonim) and therefore a person can even finish his shabbat meal before nightfall. The ספר רץ כצבי then says that the Sefer Chasidim/Maharshal and the Taz on the yesod of tosefet shabbat. The Sefer Chasidim/Maharshal holds that tosefet shabbat is not שייך (related) to the essence of the shabbat, therefore one can eat even before nightfall, therefore Tosefet Shabbat is a regular weekday just with melachot and things he can't do (like view 2), therefore one can't finish his meal before nightfall. But according to the Taz when one takes in shabbat early, shabbat ממש starts in all its details, even though the sun didn't set, and therefore if one finishes his shabbat meal before nightfall he is yotzei.

However in our case, there is a melacha being done before shabbat “really came in” and the question is if nolad would apply. According to the above chakirah, everyone agrees that there is issur melacha for someone who takes in shabbat early as mentioned in Shulchan Aruch O.C. Siman 263. However the special thing about tosefet shabbat is that one can ask another Jew to do a melacha for him as mentioned there in Seif 17.

Intro to the next part:

The reason that a Jew who accepted shabbat early can do melacha for you is for two main reasons: 1) The Eliyah Rabah O.C. Siman 263 Seif Katan 38 quoting the Beit Yosef says, אי בעי לא היה מקבל שבת עליו, meaning that its allowed since if he wanted to, he didn't need to accept shabbat. 2) The second reason is in the Kaf Hachaim quoting the Taz in Seif Katan 101 who says מיהו הט"ז סק"ג כתב הטעם כיוון דלחבירו מותר ואין עליו איסור שבת מותר לזה האמירה דלא נאסר אמירה אלא בדבר שהוא שוה לכל ישראל, that the amira (saying something) is not assur unless its equally assur to all to klal yisrael.

The answer:

So with regards to nolad, if as we said by a regular melacha one who accepts shabbat early cannot directly get pleasure from the melacha himself but can ask someone else to give him the pleasure, the same would apply by nolad that if someone already accepted shabbat early he can’t benefit from it directly, but he can ask someone else to give him the pleasure. That would lead us to conclude that someone who accepted shabbat early cannot benefit from nolad that occurred because that's tantamount to him benefiting from the melacha himself.

Hope this answers it!

questions.title_en: Question about ‘chazak ve-emotz’
questions.question:
Shalom.

I am aware this is a stupid question, but is ‘chazak ve-emotz’ - Be strong and of a good courage in doing mitzvot a general commandment, given to all, or was it only for Yehoshua Ha-Navi?

Thanks for your time.

answers.text:
Rashi explains that the commandments was 1) given to Yehoshua in the physical sense, i.e. warfare, 2) And it was said in reference to the Torah, as He states: ‘To preserve, to act in accordance with all the laws of the Torah.’

The Gemara in Berachos 32b explains, in line with what Rashi teaches, that "Chazak VeOmetz - Be strong and of a good courage" refers to the observance of all of Torah.

do not deviate to the right or to the left, that you may succeed wherever you go” (Joshua 1:7). In this verse, observe refers to Torah study and do refers to good deeds (Maharsha); the apparently repetitive language is not extraneous. The Gemara derives: Be strong in Torah and be courageous in good deeds. (Sefaria-translation with commentary)

It is also said elsewhere in what is a reference to everyone not only Yehoshua.

חֲ֭זַק וְיַאֲמֵ֣ץ לִבֶּ֑ךָ וְ֝קַוֵּ֗ה אֶל־יְהֹ said in Tehillim 27:14 is more likely to be the source the source of the common expression of chazak V'Amatz than the pesukim in Yeshoua as it is more well known and said twice daily in Elul.

Rashi Tehillim 130:5 also quotes it in relation to being a part of the meaning of קויתי ה' קותה נפשי Tehillim 130:5 that also is not referring to only Yehoshua
